primary_root_cause: Damaged, corroded, or high-resistance CKP sensor wiring/connector (open or shorted circuit between sensor and ECM)
other_likely_causes: Failed/degraded crankshaft position sensor (cracked housing, moisture intrusion, weak magnetic pickup)
Excessive air gap or mounting misalignment between CKP sensor and flywheel/reluctor due to worn or loose mounting hardware
Damaged or contaminated flywheel reluctor (missing/chipped teeth, debris, or metal shavings)
Corroded, loose, or oxidized ECM connector pins on the CKP circuit
Chafed or heat-damaged sensor harness contacting the engine or exhaust, causing an intermittent short
recommended_first_check: Inspect the CKP sensor connector and wiring harness for corrosion, damage, or chafing, then back-probe the circuit with a multimeter/scope to verify sensor resistance and AC signal output match factory spec while cranking
reasoning: A P0371/P0372/P0374 fault means the ECM cannot reliably read crank position, which is required for ignition timing and fuel sync, so the engine can misfire, stall unexpectedly, or fail to start entirely. Because these are wiring/connector-prone circuits exposed to vibration and road conditions, harness and connector integrity should be ruled out before condemning the sensor itself. This is high urgency since loss of a reliable timing reference can leave the rider stranded or cause an unsafe stall while riding.
